source.title: Scaling laws in wearable human activity recognition
source.authors: Tom Hoddes; Alex Bijamov; Saket Joshi; Daniel Roggen; Ali Etemad; Robert Harle; David Racz

record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law tests to wearable human activity recognition using masked-autoencoder pretraining on sensor data, and reports pretraining-loss and downstream-performance results.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's own scaling results and downstream trends. Cited scaling-law results and prior-work results are not recorded. The downstream figures plot many points, but the text does not state their individual values; rows record the stated trends and explain the aggregation.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws of held-out masked-autoencoder pretraining loss against data hours and parameter count in a new modality (wearable IMU sensor data). It also reports downstream F1 trends with scale, so its own results bear on V5, V6 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add the following: the authors also find that the loss-optimal model size grows with data while downstream F1 favours the largest model even with little data, which they attribute possibly to double descent. They conclude 'when in doubt, increase the model capacity', and recommend revisiting under-parameterized prior HAR works (suggesting at least 30M parameters) and distilling large models for on-device use.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a ViT masked-autoencoder on wearable sensor signals, varies data amount and parameter count, and trains to convergence with repeated data and a fixed 500,000 pretraining steps. It does not reproduce language-model scaling experiments or estimate compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The data-scaling exponent depends on sampling strategy: USER sampling, which adds users, produces an exponent of roughly three times greater magnitude than RANDOM sampling.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched parameter counts (5M, 20M), wider-shallower encoders give better downstream linear F1 than narrower-deeper ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture shape at fixed parameter count affects downstream performance in sensor MAE models.

fits_no_version.finding: Pretraining augmentations always improve downstream F1 and shift the F1-optimal capacity toward larger models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data augmentation changes the optimal model capacity in data-constrained pretraining.

record.problems: Downstream trend values are shown in figures without stated numeric values in the text. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the scaling fits or downstream trends. For the data-scaling fits, the specific encoder architecture is not stated.
record.rows_left_out: None. The study also reports width/depth comparisons for downstream performance and optimal capacity versus data size, but these do not measure a claim version's specified held-out pretraining-loss architecture effect or fixed-compute allocation.

untested.parts: No extrapolation from small fits to much larger runs.
Compute is not fixed and no compute-optimal allocation is estimated. Figure 6 shows the loss-optimal model size rising with data, but not at fixed compute.
Width vs depth is compared only on downstream F1, not on pretraining loss.
Image, video, fine-tuning and transfer regimes, and other sensor modalities are not tested. The data and parameter ranges are narrow (up to about 1589 hours; 1M–63M parameters).
No quantitative fit of downstream F1 against scale or against pretraining loss.
Parameter-counting conventions, fitting method, training schedule and compute-optimal splits are not varied.

missing.what: Optimal capacity vs data size: loss-optimal parameter count rises monotonically with data, while the largest model is F1-best at all data sizes. This is a divergence between pretraining loss and downstream performance.

record.verdict_notes: Scaling ranges are small (six data sizes up to about 1589 hours; 1M–63M parameters). The architecture underlying the data-scaling fits is unstated, likely best-of-grid. No uncertainty is given on the fits. Training uses a fixed 500k steps with over 100 epochs of repeated data, unlike the original token-limited regime.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests wearable HAR, not language models.
It does not fit laws on small runs and test predictions against runs orders of magnitude larger.
It does not hold compute budget fixed or estimate compute-optimal parameter and token allocations.
It compares width and depth for downstream F1, but does not test whether architecture changes affect held-out pretraining loss only slightly.

The tested setting is wearable motion-sensor HAR with masked-autoencoder pretraining. It does not test image or video models, other sensor modalities, fine-tuning or transfer regimes, or whether the same form holds across those settings.
It reports downstream F1 trends with pretraining data and model capacity, but does not quantitatively test downstream performance as a function of measured pretraining loss.

It shows that data-sampling strategy changes the fitted data exponent. It does not test sensitivity to parameter-count conventions, fitting methods, or training schedules, compute-optimal splits, or systematic bending away from a power law.

relationships.condition: Wearable phone IMU data, ViT masked autoencoder trained to convergence on repeated data
relationships.reason: Pretraining test loss follows power laws in data hours in every fold and sampling strategy (R1–R10), and in parameter count (R11). Exponents are small (0.015–0.052) and the ranges are narrow.
relationships.display_finding: Test loss follows power laws in data hours across every fold and sampling strategy and in parameter count, with exponents 0.015–0.052 over narrow ranges.

source_check.reason: Table 2 gives power-law data fits for all five folds and both sampling strategies (R1–R10); Section 4.2 explicitly reports a parameter-count power-law fit in Figure 3 (R11).

relationships.condition: UCI HAR and WISDM Phone linear evaluation
relationships.reason: Best linear-eval F1 rises consistently with pretraining data and with parameter count (R12, R13, R15, R16). This is shown only in figures, with no fitted law.
relationships.display_finding: Best linear-evaluation F1 increased consistently with both pretraining data and parameter size, without a fitted scaling law.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: UCI HAR and WISDM Phone linear evaluation
source_check.reason: Section 4.3 reports consistent downstream improvement with data and increasing capacity, supporting the trends attributed to R12, R13, R15 and R16. This is qualitative scaling evidence without a fitted downstream prediction law.

relationships.condition: WISDM Watch, and loss-optimal vs F1-optimal capacity
relationships.reason: Watch gains are small (R14, R17). Per the text (Fig. 6), loss-optimal model size grows with data, but the largest model is F1-best even at minimal data, so downstream does not track pretraining loss.
relationships.display_finding: Watch gains were small, and the largest model achieved the best F1 even with minimal data, whereas loss-optimal capacity increased with data.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: WISDM Watch, and loss-optimal vs F1-optimal capacity
source_check.reason: Section 4.4 and Figure 6 show different loss-optimal and UCI HAR F1-optimal capacities, qualifying prediction from pretraining loss. Watch performance improves consistently; its reported 0.5-percentage-point gain is against training from scratch, rather than a quantified scaling slope for R14 or R17.

relationships.condition: USER vs RANDOM data sampling across five folds
relationships.reason: Fitted data exponents are about 3x larger for USER (0.044–0.052) than RANDOM (0.015–0.020) sampling, so the law depends on data composition (R1–R10).
relationships.display_finding: Across five folds, USER sampling yielded data exponents of 0.044–0.052 versus RANDOM sampling's 0.015–0.020, approximately a threefold difference.

source_check.reason: R1–R10 match Table 2: exponent magnitudes are 0.044–0.052 for USER and 0.015–0.020 for RANDOM. Section 4.2 attributes the roughly threefold difference to data diversity.
